parole.testo: 14th century, from Middle French acabit, acabie (“kind, sort”, in one instance also “accident”), of unknown origin. Possibly from Old Occitan *acabit, past participle of acabir, itself a byform of two different verbs: 1.) cabir (“to contain, comprise”), from Latin capere, and 2.) acabar (“to finish,
Inherited from Old French affre, afre, from Old Occitan affre (“horror”), from Gothic *𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍂𐍃 (*aifrs), from Proto-Germanic *aibraz (“horrible, terrible”).

parole.significato: egret (Any of various wading birds of the genera Egretta or Ardea)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan aigreta, diminutive of aigron (“heron”).
Likely borrowed from Old Occitan aiga marina, though the name is unattested. Compare Catalan aiguamarina
Borrowed from Old Occitan aiguiera, from Vulgar Latin *aquāria, from Latin aquārius. See also évier.
Inherited from Old French ambler, borrowed from Old Occitan amblar, from Latin ambulāre. Doublet of ambuler, and partially of aller.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Old Occitan anchoia (modern Occitan anchòia), from Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Latin aphyē (“small fry”), from Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē).
Borrowed from Old Occitan alberga (“camp, hut”), from Frankish *harjabergu, composed of the elements *harjaz (“army”) and *berganą (“to shelter, to protect”). Doublet of albergue.
Borrowed from Old Occitan [Term?], from Latin abrotonum. Doublet of abrotone.
Borrowed from Old Occitan badau, from badar, from Medieval Latin badare (“to gape, yawn”), probably ultimately imitative of yawning or gaping. Related to English abash.

Attested since the 1580s, from Old Occitan bagassa (“whore”), from Gallo-Roman *bacassa ("servant"). Some scholars previously postulated an origin in Arabic بَاغِيَة (bāḡiya, “prostitute”), from بَغَاء (baḡāʔ), but this was doubted by Émile Littré and is now considered unlikely.
Borrowed from Old Occitan bancal, from Medieval Latin bancālis, from the base of Proto-Germanic *bankiz + -alis.

parole.significato: band, group, gang, troupe (of people, etc)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan banda (“regiment of troops”), of Germanic origin, from Proto-West Germanic *banda or Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍅𐌰 (bandwa), ultimately from the same source as Etymology 1 above.
Borrowed from Old Occitan barrica, from Vulgar Latin *barrica (“barrel, cask”), from Gaulish *baril (“cask, barrel”); perhaps related to the source of Vulgar Latin *barra.
From basane + -er, from Old Occitan besana, basana, from Old Spanish vatanna (modern badana), from Andalusian Arabic [script needed] (baṭána), from Arabic بِطَانَة (biṭāna, “inside, lining, liner”).
Unknown, main proposals include Old Occitan.
From Old Occitan bigorna, from Latin bicornis. Doublet of bicorne.

parole.significato: Bordelais (native or inhabitant of the city of Bordeaux, Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France) (usually male)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan Bordel (Occitan Bordèu, Catalan Bordeus) + French -ais, -ois.
From Old Occitan Bordel (Occitan Bordèu, Catalan Bordeus) + French -ais, -ois.

parole.significato: ton, register ton (unit of a ship's capacity equal to 100 cubic feet)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Old Occitan bota, from Latin buttis (“bottle”).

parole.significato: canal, strait or similar narrow passage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan boca. Doublet of bouche.
Borrowed from Old Occitan borgada, from borc (“settlement, town”) + -ada. By surface analysis, bourg + -ade. Compare Italian borgata.
Inherited from Middle French boutique, borrowed from Old Occitan botica, from Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē). Doublet of bodéga.

Inherited from Middle French bramer, from Old Occitan bramar, from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌼𐌼𐍉𐌽 (*brammōn), *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (*bramjan), from Proto-Germanic *bramjaną (“to bellow, roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem-. Compare Middle Low German brammen (“to roar”), Dutch brommen (“to bellow”), English brim. More at b
From Middle French cabane (14th c.), from Old Occitan cabana, from Late Latin capanna, which see. Doublet of cabine. Perhaps also related with cahute.
From Old Occitan cabas, a word of Iberian origin (compare Catalan cabàs, Old Galician-Portuguese cabaz, Spanish capazo).
Inherited from Middle French cade, intruded around 1500 from Old Occitan cade, from Latin catanum.
Borrowed from Old Occitan capdel (“ornament”), from Latin capitellum. Doublet of cadet, caudillo, and chapiteau.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cadenat, from Late Latin catēnātum, derived from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chaîné.

parole.significato: French coinage issued in the time of Philippe de Valois, where the monarch is pictured seated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan cadera, cadieira, from Latin cathedra (“chair”). Doublet of cathèdre, chaire, and chaise.
From Old Occitan canha + -ard.

From Middle French cahut(t)e, from Old French quahute, chahute (13th c.). Further origin unknown. The main question is whether Middle Dutch kayhute (mid-15th c., modern kajuit) is from French or vice versa. However, the dating, non-initial stress, and lack of plausible Germanic derivations all point
Borrowed from Old Occitan caissa, from Latin capsa, with the common suffix -ette.
From Old Occitan caisson, from caissa. By surface analysis, caisse + -on.
Borrowed from Old Occitan calar, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō).
Inherited from Old French camail, a borrowing from Old Occitan capmalh.

parole.significato: country (the country, rural area, as opposed to the town or city), countryside
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan campanha or Old Northern French campaigne, corresponding to Old French champa(i)gne. Doublet of Champagne and champagne.

parole.significato: canton (of Switzerland, France, Luxembourg or Bosnia-Herzegovina)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French canton, from Old French canton (from the 1240s), from Old Occitan canton (“corner; canton”) (recorded before 1218), adopted in Occitan from North Italian (Gallo-Italic, early Lombard) cantone (“edge, corner; canton”), ultimately representing Latin cant- (“rim (of a wheel
Borrowed from Old Occitan capa, from Late Latin cappa (compare the inherited doublet chape; cf. also the Old Northern French variant cape).
Borrowed from Old Occitan cardon, from Medieval Latin cardō, from Latin carduus (“thistle”). Doublet of chardon and carde.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cargueson, from cargar (cognate with French charger).
Borrowed from Old Occitan carriola, from carri (“chariot”), from Vulgar Latin *carreum, variant of carrus.

Inherited from Middle French carriere. Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or Italian carriera, itself from Old Occitan, from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet charrière.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cazerna, from Latin quaterna (neuter plural of Latin quaternus). Doublet of cahier, inherited from Latin, and quaterne, a later borrowing.
Probably borrowed from Old Occitan cassonada. See casson + -ade.

parole.significato: cicada (any of several insects of the order Hemiptera)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan cigala, from Vulgar Latin *cicāla, from Latin cicāda.
From Old Occitan coffin, from Latin cophinus, from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos). Doublet of coffre.

parole.significato: breastplate (piece of armour covering the chest and sometimes the back)
parole.testo: From Old French cuirace, probably borrowed from Old Occitan coirassa, or Italian corazza, or Old Aragonese cuyraça, from Late Latin coriacea (vestis) (“leather (garment)”), from coriaceus, ultimately from Latin corium, and probably influenced by cuir in French. Doublet of coriace.

From Middle French dansielle, donselle, donzelle, from Old French donzele, borrowed from Old Occitan donçela, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, from earlier *dominicella (literally “little maidenly (woman)”), from Classical Latin domina (“mistress”) + -ica + -ella. Compare also Italian donzella, Old Oc
Probably borrowed from Old Occitan dralho, variant form of traio, from Vulgar Latin *trāgla, from Latin trāgula.
Inherited from Middle French dosme, from (Old Provençal) Old Occitan doma, borrowed from Late Latin dōma (“roof, housetop”), from Koine Greek δῶμα (dôma, “roof, housetop”) previously meaning "house".
Possibly from en- + tref, or borrowed from Old Occitan entravar, from trau, from Latin trabem.

parole.significato: moneybag (bag, normally with a drawstring, used for holding money)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan escarcella, from Italian scarsella (“purse”).
From Old Occitan fat, from Latin fatuus.
Inherited from Old French figue, borrowed from Old Occitan figa, from Vulgar Latin *fīca, from Latin ficus.

parole.significato: flute (woodwind instrument consisting of a tube with a row of holes that produce sound through vibrations caused by air…
parole.testo: From Old French fleüte, from Old Occitan flaut. The contraction of the Old French hiatus created a long vowel in Middle French, which is indicated by the modern circumflex.

Inherited from Middle French fougasse, foucasse, borrowed from Old Occitan fogatza, fogassa, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Doublet of the inherited fouace.

parole.significato: youthful prank, escapade (with a notion of indulgence)
parole.testo: Probably from Old Occitan fradin.
Inherited from Middle French fustet, from Old Occitan fustet, from Arabic فُسْتَق (fustaq) with Occitanized ending.
From Old Occitan gaf (“clasp”), from Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍆𐌰𐌷 (gafah, “clasp”, noun), from 𐌲𐌰- (ga-, intensifier) + 𐍆𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (fahan, “to catch”).
From Latin gȳrus (“circle”) + -ole, or possibly an adaptation of Old Occitan giroilla, from a diminutive of gir, from the same Latin root.
From Old French gobel, from Old Occitan gobel (“to swallow up”), from Gaulish *gobbos, from Proto-Celtic *gobbos (“muzzle, snout, beak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵoph₃o- (“eat”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; obscure; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French gousse, from Old French gose, gosse (“bean pod, hull, husk”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old Occitan gossa (“female dog, bitch”), from gos (“dog”), however the sense evolution is obscure; for similar semantic development, compare French caïeu (“clove of garlic”),
Derived from Old French or Old Occitan, both from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Akin to Old High German grīs (“grey”) (German greis) and Dutch grijs (“grey”). More at grizzle.

From Old French guide, borrowed from Old Occitan guida, from the verb guidar, ultimately of Germanic origin, possibly through Medieval Latin; compare Frankish *wītan. Supplanted the older Old French guier, of the same origin. Compare Italian guida, Spanish guía. See guider for more information.
Borrowed from Old Occitan irondela, diminutive of irunda, ironda, ultimately from Latin hirundō. Replaced Old French arondelle, diminutive of aronde, from Latin hirundō (compare also harundō).

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French jazerant, from Old Occitan jazerenc, from Arabic جَزَائِرِيّ (jazāʔiriyy, “Algerian, of Algiers”), derived from الجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir, “Algiers; Algeria”).
Inherited from Old French jurat, borrowed from Old Occitan jurat, from Latin iūrātus. Doublet of juré, which was inherited.

Inherited from Old French langouste, languste, borrowed from Old Occitan langosta, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Cf. also the Old French laöste, laüste, laouste, which was inherited from the Latin, as well as locuste, which was a learned borrowing.
Probably from Old Occitan lentiscle, from Late Latin *lentisculus, diminutive of Latin lentiscus.
Earlier loriol, by rebracketing from Old French oriol, from Old Occitan auriol, from Latin aureolus (“golden”).

Inherited from Middle French lut, from Old French leüt, leüz, probably borrowed from Old Occitan laüt or laütz, from Arabic اَلْعُود (al-ʕūd, “wood”); possibly through the intermediate of Old Spanish alod, alaut, laúd.
From Old Occitan madier, from Late Latin materium, from Latin materia.
Borrowed from Old Occitan milan, from Vulgar Latin *mīlānus, alteration of Latin mīlvinus, from mīlvus.
Borrowed from Old Occitan maestral (whence Occitan mistral) from Late Latin magistrālis, from Latin magister. Doublet of magistral.

parole.significato: barnacle, twitch, a kind of pincers or vise to fix the mouth of a horse to yield the opportunity of surgery
parole.testo: From Old Occitan moralha, from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”), the like source as in morion (“a kind of helmet with no visor”), moraine (“amassment of rocks on a glacier”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan muscada, from musc. See also muguet and muscat.
Borrowed from Old Occitan mejer (compare modern Occitan miegé, miegié, megié, megé), itself from a Late Latin mediārius or derived from meg, from Latin medius (“middle, half”).
Probably from Old Occitan palafrenier.

Inherited from Middle French parfum, from parfumer (“to scent”), borrowed from Old Occitan perfumar or another language around the Mediterranean coast, cf. Italian profumare, themselves from Latin per (“through, thoroughly”) + fumāre (“to smoke”).
Inherited from Middle French parfumer, probably borrowed from Old Occitan parfumer or Italian perfumare, from Latin per- + fumāre.
Inherited from Middle French pastenade, pastinade, from Old Occitan pastenaga (“carrot”), from Latin pastinaca. Doublet of panais.
Borrowed from Old Occitan pastenago, pastenaga (“parsnip”), from Latin pastinaca. Doublet of panais.
From Old Occitan pinhon, from pinha (“pine-cone”).
Inherited from Old French pimper, from Old Occitan pimpar, of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps expressive.

parole.significato: to pimp out/pimp up, to beautify, to fancify, to make stylish, to make gaudy
parole.testo: From English to pimp (African-American Vernacular) + -er, from Old French pimper, from Old Occitan pimpar (see above).

parole.significato: Any of a large variety of scorpaeniform fishes, such as certain lionfishes and stonefishes.
parole.testo: From Old Occitan rascas (“worm-ridden; filthy”).
Borrowed from Old Occitan radel, a diminutive of rat, itself from Latin ratis (“raft”).
Calque of Old Occitan retaule. Compare Catalan retaule.

From Old Occitan rossinhol (cf. Catalan rossinyol), from Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, masculine diminutive of Latin luscinia (“nightingale”). According to De Vaan, "might be explained with haplology from *lusci-cania (“singing in the night; blind singer”), but this is conjecture.
Borrowed from Old Occitan sabina.
Borrowed from Old Occitan sorba, from Vulgar Latin *sorba, feminine singular formed from the plural of Latin sorbum.
Ultimately from Old Occitan sorn (“dark”).
From Old Occitan sota, originally a preposition, from Late Latin subtus (“under”).
From terre, probably influenced by Old Occitan terrassa.
Alteration of tamballe (as though formed from cimbale + timbre), from Old Occitan tambala, from Arabic طَبْل (ṭabl).
Inherited from Old French toquesain, borrowed from Old Occitan tocasenh, from tocar (“strike, touch”) + senh (“bell”).

Inherited from Middle French tortue, borrowed from Old Occitan tortuga, tartuga, from Late Latin tartarūcha, feminine form of tartarūchus, a mythological spirit of Greek origin, from Ancient Greek ταρταροῦχος (tartaroûkhos, “resident or native of Tartarus”), from Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Cf. also Mediev
Borrowed from Old Occitan trobador (< trobar (“to find”)) via Old French troubadour. Corresponds to the native French trouveur.
From Middle French truc, from Old French trut, borrowed from Old Occitan truc, deverbal from trucar, from Vulgar Latin *trūdicāre.
From Old Occitan trufa, ultimately from Latin tuber.

Inherited from Old French vignoble (also latinised as vinoblium). According to the most widely accepted theory from Old Occitan vinhobre, from Vulgar Latin *vineoporus, from Ancient Greek ἀμπελoφόρος (ampelophóros, “bearing vines”) by substitution of the component word ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “vine”) with

parole.significato: a magistrate that administered a viguerie
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan, from Latin vicārius. Doublet of voyer and vicaire.
Inherited from Old French [Term?], probably from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), from Medieval Latin *vitula (“stringed instrument”). Compare Italian viola.
Inherited from Middle French escueil, borrowed from Old Occitan escueyll, from Vulgar Latin *scoculum, from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek. Cognate with Italian scoglio.

Inherited from Old French espagneul, espaigneul, a Gallicization of Old Occitan espaignol (“Spanish”), from Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus (“Spanish”), from Hispānia (“Spain”). First used as Espainholz in the 14th century by Gaston III of Foix, who described them in a book on hunting. An alternative theo

parole.significato: shelf (flat, rigid structure, fixed at right angles to a wall or forming a part of a cabinet, desk, etc., and used to s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan estagiera (modern Occitan estatgiera).
